dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — it's homecoming day: Benji is expected to be discharged today, with his first pediatrician appointment already booked for tomorrow, and Solon is giving you a beautiful day for it, mostly sunny with a high near 73°. It is also Election Day: Ohio polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM, the governor's race between Amy Acton and Vivek Ramaswamy and the Senate race between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown are both close, and 66 Cuyahoga County precincts — including some in Solon — have new polling places, so check yours before you go. Overnight the U.S. carried out limited strikes on Iranian missile targets on Qeshm Island while talks remained possible, and the Cavs lost a close one to Oklahoma City, 117-112, despite the game staying tight into the final minute. Tonight, after the ride home and a first evening as a family of four (plus Moose), the results start rolling in after Ohio polls close at 7:30.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
U.S. hits Iranian missile targets on Qeshm Island on election eve, while saying a deal is still possible
items.summary:
The U.S. military struck Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, with Iranian state television reporting explosions on Qeshm Island. A U.S. official, speaking anonymously, said the targets were Iranians who had used surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets, and other reporting said the strikes followed Iran firing at a U.S. aircraft.

The strikes were described as limited and defensive, not a return to full-scale fighting, and they appear to be part of a series of smaller strikes in recent weeks. They came even though President Trump had previously said the U.S. would not launch new attacks before Tuesday's vote — and when asked Monday whether he was considering strikes after the midterms, he answered no.

At the same time, Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism about a negotiated settlement, saying there had been good conversations with Iran. The war is now in its ninth month, the U.S. still maintains a naval blockade, and Tehran says the strait could reopen quickly if the blockade and new sanctions are lifted — terms Washington has not accepted.

Watch whether the strikes stay limited after Election Day, and whether mediated talks produce anything concrete on reopening Hormuz to shipping.

items.title: Russian double strike on a Ukrainian aid school kills 26, including rescuers and police
items.summary:
At least 26 people were killed Monday when Russian aerial bombs hit a school in the village of Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and emergency services said. Among the dead were two rescue workers and four police officers, and several people were treated in hospital.

No classes were being held at the school because it sits close to the front line. Instead, residents gathered there every Monday to shelter and collect humanitarian aid packages — a predictable weekly routine. Zelenskiy said a first strike hit as people arrived and a second hit the shelter, a pattern often called a double strike.

The attack came a day after a short local ceasefire, arranged to bring aid into a neighbouring area and evacuate residents, had expired. Zelenskiy argued Russia had passed up a chance to extend humanitarian steps, while rescue teams worked through smouldering rubble looking for people still trapped.

Watch for the final toll as the rubble is cleared, and for whether the attack hardens positions ahead of the peace talks scheduled in Abu Dhabi next week.

items.title: Oil plunges nearly 8% as traders bet the U.S. and Iran might talk instead of escalating
items.summary:
Oil prices tumbled on Monday, with Brent crude falling about 7.6% and U.S. crude dropping about 7.4% in its biggest decline in three months. By Tuesday in Singapore, Brent was holding near $104.77 a barrel and U.S. crude was below $97.

The drop came as both Washington and Tehran signalled a willingness to pursue peace talks as the war enters its ninth month. Iran's president said his government had been given more authority to negotiate, and President Trump hinted at progress — even as U.S. forces struck targets on Qeshm Island the same day.

Monday's fall partly reversed a strong October, when Brent rose almost 14% to a six-month high on fears of renewed fighting. European gas futures also fell sharply, and U.S. heating oil posted its steepest drop in six months.

The gap between the two sides is still wide: Tehran wants the naval blockade lifted, sanctions eased and frozen assets released, while Washington wants concessions on Iran's nuclear programme. Analysts warn prices could jump back quickly if attacks intensify.

items.title: U.S., Ukraine and Russia will meet in Abu Dhabi next week for a new round of peace talks
items.summary:
The Kremlin confirmed Tuesday that Russia will hold three-way talks with Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to President Vladimir Putin, will lead Moscow's delegation.

U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said Monday the meeting would bring Ukrainian and Russian delegations together to discuss post-war security arrangements and ways to de-escalate. Earlier reporting said lead U.S. negotiators are expected to include Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with humanitarian measures also on the agenda.

The war is now in its fifth year, and U.S. negotiators have been looking for a breakthrough before winter. The last U.S.-mediated talks took place in February, before the war against Iran pulled Washington's attention elsewhere. Putin agreed to this new round after meeting Witkoff in St. Petersburg two weeks ago.

Watch who Ukraine sends, and whether any ceasefire or de-escalation language comes out of the two days in Abu Dhabi.

items.title: Cargo ships are being sunk near NATO's Black Sea coast, and the alliance is being tested
items.summary:
After seven strikes on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria last month, NATO said it would send patrol aircraft, radars and drones to strengthen its Black Sea flank. Three days after that pledge, another ship was struck just outside Romanian waters, and last week a Greek container ship was sunk by naval drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.

Analysts told Reuters they had little doubt the attacks were Russian, though Russia denies targeting Ukraine's neighbours. One count found 317 merchant and other vessels hit in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov between May and October, up sharply from 74 in the previous half-year.

The disruption has hit trade hard. Ukraine suspended Black Sea port operations in late July and diverted exports to Danube river ports, and its port grain exports in September were less than half the level of a year earlier. Russia's own Black Sea grain exports fell even more sharply.

NATO calls the attacks a serious security threat aimed at discouraging support for Ukraine. Watch for any stronger alliance response, movement on a narrow maritime ceasefire, and further strikes in Romanian or Bulgarian waters.

items.title: New Zealand election is neck-and-neck — neither side can govern without a small centrist party
items.summary:
New Zealand's final major poll before Saturday's election puts the ruling conservative National Party at 30% and the centre-left opposition Labour Party at 29% — effectively a dead heat days before voters go to the polls. The Greens rose to 16%, while National's current coalition partners, ACT and NZ First, both slipped.

The numbers leave neither side able to govern on its own. A right-leaning bloc of National, ACT and NZ First falls short, and so does a left bloc of Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori. Both would need support from the centrist Opportunity Party, unchanged at 6%.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional system tends to produce coalition governments, so negotiation is normal — but this time one small centrist party looks set to become the kingmaker for whoever forms the next government.

Watch Saturday's seat count first, then how quickly coalition talks with Opportunity begin.

items.title: Today decides who controls Congress — but the winner might not be clear for days
items.summary:
Tuesday's midterm vote will decide which party controls Congress for the final two years of President Trump's second term. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are being contested, and 36 states are electing governors.

Republicans currently hold the Senate 53-47 and a narrow House lead. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats and three House seats to take both chambers. Forecasters have been predicting a strong Democratic night in the House, while the Senate map is full of toss-ups. A record number of Americans — roughly 57 million by one count — had already voted early.

The answer may not come tonight. Control could be clear late Tuesday, or it could take more than a week if key races are close. California is famously slow to count, and Alaska's ranked-choice system and possible litigation could add delays there.

The first polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. Ohio's polls close at 7:30 p.m., and the big wave of Senate results arrives around 9 p.m.

items.title: Watch Kentucky, Indiana, Florida and Virginia early tonight — they will tell you who is winning the House
items.summary:
Democrats are strongly favoured to win a House majority tonight, but the earliest returns will show whether the night is close or a rout. Operatives on both sides are watching a handful of races that report first.

In Kentucky's 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado for a seat left open by a senator-bound incumbent, with polls closing at 6 p.m. Eastern. At the same hour in Indiana's 5th District, Republican Victoria Spartz defends a solidly red seat against Democrat J.D. Ford — a Ford win there would signal a very big Democratic night.

Florida then offers Republicans their best early hope: redistricting put four Democratic-held seats in play, and a Republican path to holding the House likely runs through flipping them. In Virginia, two Republican-held districts — the 1st and the 2nd — are potential Democratic pickups on the state's existing map.

If Democrats flip the Kentucky or Indiana seats early, the wave is real. If Republicans take the Florida seats, their path to keeping the majority stays alive.

items.title: Supreme Court refuses to sideline 20,000 California ballots the Trump administration questioned
items.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined the Justice Department's emergency request to force California to set aside midterm ballots cast by about 20,000 registered voters the administration alleges may not be citizens. The court gave no reasoning, and no justice publicly dissented.

Lower courts had already ruled against the administration. A district judge wrote that the federal government had never before, on the eve of an election, tried to force a state to abandon its own election procedures, and questioned how the list of names was built. An appeals panel said using the list could block valid votes and jeopardise Los Angeles County's election.

California says it already has safeguards against noncitizen voting, and called the administration's list-building process highly suspect. The Constitution gives states and Congress — not the executive branch — the main role in regulating federal elections.

California will count its ballots under its normal procedures today. The underlying Justice Department lawsuit against the state is still pending, so the fight is not over even after the votes are counted.

items.title: Ohio could decide the Senate — and its governor's race is just as tight
items.summary:
Ohio is at the centre of tonight's map, with one of the country's most competitive governor's races, a Senate contest that could shape control of the chamber, and House races that could matter for the majority. Hundreds of millions of dollars have flowed into the state.

For governor, Trump-backed entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, the former state health director. Neither has won a political race before, Ohio has not elected a Democratic governor since 2006, and the winner will make history either way — as the state's first woman elected governor, or its first person of colour elected to the job. Final polls from different pollsters gave Acton a lead of between four and eight points.

For the Senate, Republican Jon Husted faces former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who is attempting a comeback after losing in 2024. More than $500 million in advertising has been spent on the race, and Democrats see Ohio as one of their best chances to flip a seat.

Ohio's polls close at 7:30 p.m. Eastern. Watch the Senate margin first, then whether Acton can break her party's 20-year drought in the governor's office.

items.title: Texas Democrat closes by attacking Elon Musk's huge spending for his opponent
items.summary:
Texas Senate candidate James Talarico closed his campaign Monday night in Austin by making Elon Musk the centre of his pitch. Musk, the world's richest man and a Texas resident, has put more than $160 million into the race to support Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Total spending in the race has passed half a billion dollars, making it one of the most expensive non-presidential races in U.S. history. Talarico himself raised a record $64 million in a single quarter. There was no debate — the first Texas Senate race without one since 2000.

Paxton won the Republican nomination by defeating incumbent Senator John Cornyn, the first Texas incumbent senator to lose renomination since 1970. Polls disagree on the general election: one late survey had Talarico ahead by seven points, another had the race tied.

Democrats have not won a Texas Senate election since 1988, and have not won any statewide race in Texas since 1994. A Talarico win would be a generational breakthrough — and a key step toward the Senate majority.

items.title: Trump spent his final pre-election speech on D.C. renovations and a $5,000 promise, while polls favour Democrats
items.summary:
Standing before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday, President Trump spent more than 20 minutes of his closing midterm speech on Washington construction projects — the pool's repairs, a new helipad, park improvements and a planned triumphal arch — before turning to the election itself.

When he did address the vote, he warned against the Democratic slate and repeated his promise of a $5,000 payment to every adult citizen if Republicans keep control of both the House and the Senate.

The focus was striking because voters say their top concern is the cost of living, and final forecasts favour Democrats. One ratings service counts 222 House districts leaning Democratic — more than the 218 needed for a majority — and late Senate polls showed Democrats leading in most of the contested states. Trump's approval rating was 37% in one poll cited in the coverage, described as a new low.

Trump will spend Election Day out of public view and host a viewing reception at the White House tonight. Watch whether the $5,000 pledge is revived or quietly dropped once the results are known.

items.title: Apple beats forecasts with a record September quarter, but its stock still falls
items.summary:
Apple reported record September-quarter results on Monday: revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, and earnings of $2.10 a share, up 14%. Both beat Wall Street's expectations, and iPhone revenue set a September-quarter record at $57.58 billion.

Services revenue hit an all-time high of $31.57 billion, with paid subscriptions passing 1.5 billion. Mac sales jumped 24%, while iPad revenue fell about 10%. For the full fiscal year, Apple's revenue reached a record $479 billion. New CEO John Ternus, who took over September 1, led the earnings call.

Investors focused instead on what comes next. Apple guided December-quarter growth of 7-10% with thinner profit margins, its China revenue came in below expectations, and its shares fell in after-hours and premarket trading despite the beat.

It is a sign of the current mood: even a record quarter is not enough if the outlook slows. Apple's AI features begin testing in China this week, which will be one story to follow.

items.title: Nasdaq slips into correction as investors question the cost of the AI boom
items.summary:
The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.39% on Monday to about 10.4% below its October 6 all-time high — its third technical correction of 2026, even though it is still up about 11% for the year. Chip stocks were hit hardest, with the semiconductor benchmark down about 12% in three sessions.

The broader market split: the Dow rose 0.41% on Monday while the S&P 500 fell 0.51% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.07%. Oracle dropped about 9% after filing to raise $20 billion — half in stock, half in bonds — to fund its AI and cloud buildout. Asian markets followed the slide, with South Korea and Taiwan down about 3.6% each.

The shift is about questions, not collapse. Investors are moving from rewarding AI potential to asking what the spending earns back, and even strong results from Apple and Palantir did not lift their shares.

Futures were mixed on Election Day morning, a tentative sign the selloff could pause. Chipmaker AMD reports later today and will be the next test of AI sentiment.

items.title: Palantir revenue jumps 96% as business customers pass government for the first time
items.summary:
Palantir's third-quarter revenue jumped 96% from a year earlier to $2.313 billion — its first quarter above $2 billion — beating expectations. Profit reached $1.128 billion, and the company closed 212 deals worth at least $1 million each.

The milestone was in the mix. U.S. commercial revenue rose 148% to $984 million, passing U.S. government revenue of $953 million for the first time in the company's history. U.S. revenue overall was $1.937 billion, 84% of the total.

Palantir raised its full-year guidance to about $8.53 billion and lifted its outlook for U.S. commercial sales and for the fourth quarter, both above what analysts expected.

Even so, the stock fell — closing down about 3% Monday and slipping further after hours. Analysts pointed to slower growth in the total value of new U.S. commercial contracts, a reminder that in this market a beat alone no longer guarantees a rally.

items.title: Anthropic posts a $17 billion quarter ahead of its IPO, but spending commitments are huge
items.summary:
Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of about $17 billion, up more than 1,100% from a year earlier, in an updated filing ahead of its planned public offering. Revenue for the first nine months of the year was $33.24 billion.

Growth is still enormous but slowing in percentage terms: revenue rose 47% in the third quarter, after gains of 144% and 132% in the two quarters before it. The company also swung back to an operating loss of $567 million in the quarter.

The eye-catching number is on the spending side. The filing lists about $895 billion in purchase commitments and leases, almost all for computing power and infrastructure, and its computing costs grew 382% in a year. Short-term computing commitments were a main driver of the operating loss.

Anthropic says its Claude system has seen the fastest business adoption of any technology in history. Investors in the IPO will have to decide how much of that spending turns into lasting profit.

items.title: Marvell to buy Lumentum for $115 billion in one of the biggest tech deals ever
items.summary:
Marvell Technology has agreed to buy Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion including debt, announced Monday — one of the largest technology deals ever, bigger than Microsoft's purchase of Activision Blizzard and Dell's purchase of EMC.

Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each share they own, a premium of about 24%, and will own roughly a third of the combined company. Both boards approved the deal unanimously. Marvell's CEO stays in charge, and three Lumentum directors will join the board.

The logic is AI data centres. Marvell makes custom chips and electrical connections; Lumentum makes the lasers and optical parts that move data with light. Together they project more than $1 billion in annual cost savings and a combined market opportunity of $550 billion. Nvidia invested $2 billion in each company earlier this year.

The deal is not expected to close until the first half of 2028, pending shareholder and regulatory approval — a long road for a merger this size.

items.title: CrowdStrike to buy two AI security startups for $495 million to police AI agents
items.summary:
CrowdStrike will pay a combined $495 million for two artificial-intelligence security startups, expanding its push to monitor AI agents as companies deploy them widely. The larger deal is Fiddler AI, at about $400 million, whose software watches and explains what AI agents are doing.

The second purchase, Dreadnode at about $95 million, makes automated testing tools that probe AI models for weaknesses before they are released — including more than 100 attack strategies such as jailbreaks and prompt injection.

CrowdStrike plans to sell Fiddler's tools as Falcon Observe, alongside a Falcon Guardian feature that works like a kill switch, letting administrators shut down an agent that starts behaving abnormally. Its president said companies are well past the testing phase and are deploying agents at scale now.

The risk CrowdStrike is targeting is not only outside attackers, but agents that are set up wrong or given too much access. Both deals are expected to close in the company's fiscal fourth quarter.

items.title: Election Day arrives after a surge in early voting, with observers watching the polls closely
items.summary:
The final day of midterm voting opened Tuesday after millions of Americans had already cast ballots early — more than 50 million by one Associated Press count — putting turnout on pace to pass the last midterms. Voting so far had unfolded with relatively few problems, the AP reported.

The Justice Department is running its largest-ever Election Day effort to monitor polling places. Democrats and allied groups have fielded an even larger effort of their own, with tens of thousands of trained volunteer observers.

Officials said no armed federal officers would guard polling places, and feared steps such as immigration agents at voting sites or seized machines had not happened by Tuesday morning. The Supreme Court also declined Monday night to let the administration set aside California ballots in its search for noncitizen voters.

Weather is the practical complication in the Southwest, where weekend flash flooding may make some polling places harder to reach. Officials are urging anyone still holding an absentee ballot to drop it off in person rather than mail it.

items.title: Flash flooding forces evacuations across Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico
items.summary:
Heavy rain on Sunday produced flash flooding and mandatory evacuations across a wide stretch of the Southwest — the second major drenching in about two weeks for a normally dry region. A Tucson fire crew rescued a woman from a car stuck in a flooded wash, one of many water rescues over the weekend.

In Pagosa Springs, Colorado, officials warned of catastrophic flooding as the San Juan River rose; the river eventually crested at roughly 16.8 feet late Sunday, and roads in and out of town were closed. In Sedona, Arizona, residents near Oak Creek were ordered to leave immediately, floodwaters trapped people in homes, and helicopter rescues were reported. The community of Gisela was ordered fully evacuated.

A National Weather Service meteorologist in Tucson described it as two or three months of rain in a couple of days, with up to about four inches falling across the region. Warnings covered nearly all of Arizona plus parts of Utah, Colorado, New Mexico and Nevada.

No deaths or injuries had been reported in the AP's Sunday reporting, though nearly 20 homes in one Arizona county needed emergency relocation help. Drier weather was expected for Election Day, with cleanup and road damage lingering.

items.title: Record Southwest flooding raises the El Niño question as rivers break records
items.summary:
The weekend's flooding in the Southwest was not just heavy — in places it was record-breaking. The Little Colorado River at Woodruff beat its previous record by about six feet, and the Gila River near Solomon rose 18 feet in a day, passing its historic high by six feet.

As of Monday morning, 11 rivers in Colorado and Arizona were at or approaching major flood stage, with warnings for rockfalls, mudslides and debris flows on burn scars and in slot canyons. Durango, Colorado recorded 4.3 inches of precipitation on Sunday alone. The flooding even closed a ballot drop box in one Colorado county ahead of Election Day.

Scientists are debating the cause. One climate scientist argued that back-to-back record rain events during one of the strongest El Niño events on record is not a coincidence. A National Weather Service meteorologist cautioned that this week's weather cannot yet be attributed to El Niño.

More flooding was forecast into Tuesday in parts of Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico, even as drier weather returns. Snow is the other side of the storm, with up to a foot and a half possible in the San Juan Mountains.

items.title: Judge dismisses the administration's lawsuit seeking Harvard's admissions records
items.summary:
A federal judge in Boston on Monday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit that sought to force Harvard University to hand over records for an investigation into whether it still considers race in admissions.

The department sued in February, saying it needed years of applicant-level data to check Harvard's compliance with the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling against race-conscious admissions. The case was brought under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act.

Harvard argued the suit was retaliation for refusing administration demands to overhaul its governance, hiring and academic programmes, and noted it was filed after the president ended settlement talks and said he wanted $1 billion in damages. Harvard also said the government had sued without first following the steps required to seek voluntary compliance, and that the records involved sensitive data on thousands of high school applicants.

The ruling is the latest in a string of court losses for the administration in its fight with Harvard, which has also won cases over terminated research grants and its ability to host international students.

items.title: U.S. intelligence sharing has fractured amid agency turf wars, officials say
items.summary:
Intelligence sharing on Iran and other global threats — with Congress and across the federal government — has slowed and at times stopped during President Trump's second term, according to eight current and former officials and people briefed on the matter who spoke to Reuters.

The problems centred on deep tension between the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the CIA, described as one of the biggest turf wars in three decades. The CIA stopped co-authoring assessments with the National Intelligence Council, lawmakers briefly stopped receiving some reports at two points, and briefings to Congress on election threats were halted in 2025 before being resumed under a new intelligence director in August.

The FBI also stopped sharing some intelligence with the National Counterterrorism Center for several weeks after a dispute over an investigation. Former officials warn the gaps risk an incomplete picture of threats, echoing failures before the September 11 attacks, and some are working on bipartisan plans to rebuild the system.

The CIA and the intelligence director's office both said in response that sharing continues and assessment levels are near historic norms. The report lands as the administration weighs whether to resume strikes on Iran after the midterms.

items.title: Philips reaches a Justice Department agreement over its 2021 sleep-device recall
items.summary:
Philips Respironics has reached an agreement in principle with the U.S. Justice Department to resolve criminal and civil investigations tied to its 2021 global recall of sleep and respiratory devices.

Philips recalled millions of devices in 2021 over concerns that sound-reducing foam inside them could break down and potentially become toxic. The company has set aside 288 million euros — about $322 million — for the proposed settlement, with payment expected in early 2027 once final documents are signed.

The company did not say whether the agreement includes an admission of wrongdoing, and its CEO said the deal was reached only in the last few days. Philips also beat quarterly profit expectations and kept its 2026 financial targets unchanged.

The settlement would not end every legal thread. A separate investigation by U.S. state attorneys general is still ongoing, and Philips says those talks are too early to estimate.

items.title: Election Day in Ohio: Governor and Senate races come down to turnout in Cleveland and two bellwether counties
items.summary:
Ohio is being treated like a purple swing state today. The governor's race between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is close in the polls, and the Senate race between Republican Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown is a nailbiter that could help decide control of the Senate.

Three things will decide the night. The first is Mahoning County, around Youngstown, which flipped Republican in the Trump era — Republicans need it to stay red. The second is fast-growing Delaware County, whose presidential margins have narrowed dramatically over two decades, testing whether it is turning blue. The third is turnout in Cincinnati, Columbus and especially Cleveland, where early voting in Cuyahoga County was described as unprecedented, with lines snaking through the Board of Elections office.

Statewide, more than 1.7 million Ohioans had already voted early, a record for in-person early voting. Cuyahoga County turnout has been drifting down over the years, which is exactly why both campaigns pushed so hard to get Cleveland voters out.

Polls close at 7:30 p.m. tonight. Cleveland's turnout — particularly among Black voters — may be the margin in both statewide races.

items.title: Check your polling place: 66 precincts moved in Cuyahoga County, including Solon
items.summary:
If you are voting in person today, check your polling place first. The Cuyahoga County Board of Elections announced 66 precinct location changes across nine cities, affecting nearly 60,000 voters — and Solon is on the list.

Many of the Cleveland changes happened because the Cleveland school district closed 10 buildings that had been used as polling places. The board mailed location-change letters to every affected voter, but a letter is easy to miss in a busy week.

Polls are open today from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. You can confirm your location at boe.cuyahogacounty.gov or by calling 216-443-8683. Bring an accepted photo ID — an unexpired Ohio driver licence or state ID, a U.S. passport, or a military ID. A digital ID in Apple Wallet is not accepted.

The Board of Elections office itself is at 1803 Superior Avenue in Cleveland, which is also where Cuyahoga County voters can drop off a completed mail ballot today.

items.title: Still holding a mail ballot? Drop it off by 7:30 p.m. tonight — Ohio ended the grace period
items.summary:
Ohio's rules for mail ballots changed this year, and the change matters tonight. Under a law signed last December, an absentee ballot now has to arrive by the close of polls on Election Day to be counted — the old four-day grace period after Election Day is gone, except for military and overseas voters.

That means a ballot still sitting on your kitchen counter must be received by 7:30 p.m. today. Secretary of State Frank LaRose warned on October 27 that it was likely already too late to mail a ballot and have it arrive in time.

The safe move is to drop it off in person. For Cuyahoga County voters, that is the Board of Elections at 1803 Superior Avenue in Cleveland, which has a secure drop box.

Early in-person voting ran from October 6 through Sunday. Today is the last step: polls open 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., with the governor's race, a U.S. Senate race and the statewide offices all on the ballot.

items.title: Vance rallies Republicans near Toledo as Democrats push affordability in Columbus on election eve
items.summary:
Both parties closed their Ohio campaigns on Monday. Vice President JD Vance headlined a rally near Toledo alongside Donald Trump Jr., Vivek Ramaswamy and Jon Husted — the sixth campaign trip to Ohio by Vance or President Trump in six weeks.

Democrats held their own election-eve rally in Columbus, promising to make life more affordable and painting their opponents as beholden to special interests. Amy Acton told the crowd the race was about extreme wealth and special interests against everyone else.

The late polling in the file tells a close story. One survey had Acton ahead of Ramaswamy by about eight points for governor and Sherrod Brown ahead of Husted by about seven for the Senate; a polling average put Acton's lead closer to four points. Treat those as polls, not results.

Many of the people at both rallies had already voted — they were part of the record 1.7 million Ohioans who cast early ballots. Tonight's turnout decides whether the polling held.

items.title: Issue 3 explained: Ohio's lone statewide ballot issue would put voter photo ID in the constitution
items.summary:
Ohio has exactly one statewide issue on today's ballot. Issue 3 would write the state's voter photo ID requirement into the Ohio Constitution.

Ohio has required photo ID for in-person voting under state law since 2023, so for most voters nothing about today would feel different. The change is about permanence: a constitutional requirement is much harder for a future legislature or court to undo. The General Assembly placed the amendment on the ballot, and it takes effect immediately if a majority votes yes.

Accepted IDs include an unexpired Ohio driver licence or state ID, a U.S. passport or passport card, and military, Ohio National Guard or veterans' ID. The amendment also allows state law to provide an alternative for voters with a sincere religious objection to being photographed. Its ballot title runs about 200 words — among the longest in the country this year.

Several other proposed amendments — on property taxes, data centres and other topics — did not make the 2026 ballot, and their organisers are aiming at 2027 instead.

items.title: Cleveland voters say gas and grocery prices are driving them to vote
items.summary:
In Cleveland's Central neighbourhood, about two dozen residents at a community workshop on stress and chronic illness were handed election guides for today's vote — and the conversation kept coming back to the cost of everyday life.

Organisers with Cleveland VOTES and its Vote Squad have canvassed for months, trying to connect daily frustrations to voting. The issues they hear most are gas prices, federal cuts to food assistance, and stricter work requirements for Medicaid set to take effect next year. They also spend much of their time pushing back on the idea, still common in the neighbourhood, that a vote does not matter.

Greater Cleveland Congregations has sent door-knocking volunteers across Cleveland and its inner-ring suburbs. Its organisers say voters this year sound far more urgent about voting than in the last midterm, and that they lead with issues like gas and food.

It is a useful ground-level read on tonight: in Ohio's biggest city, affordability — not party messaging — is what is moving people to the polls.

baby.tip: Homecoming day tip: before you leave the hospital, do the car-seat check while help is still right there — base tight, straps snug at armpit level, and Benji's first ride home in a rear-facing seat in the back. Then tonight, keep it simple: one bag unpacked, feeding log started, and the diaper bag restocked for tomorrow's first pediatrician visit. If anything about feeding, breathing or temperature worries you at home, call the pediatrician or your OB team — that's exactly what they're there for.
baby.fact: Newborns sleep a lot but in short stretches — typically 16 to 17 hours a day, broken into naps of just a few hours at a time, because their tiny stomachs need frequent feeding. Benji's sleep will feel random this first week; short, frequent stretches around the clock are completely normal for a brand-new baby.
baby.fun: Today's tiny mission: the first family photo at home — Mike, Kelly, Benji and Moose in one frame (Moose at a calm, supervised distance for take one). It doesn't need to be perfect; the slightly chaotic version is the one you'll love most in a year.
